findings.summary: The Common Mistake section is prose and its fix is not tied to a visual or the earlier idea.
findings.evidence: Every feature crosses three teams and creates hand-offs. Own a slice of value instead.
findings.fix: Split into bullets: 'Layer teams: every feature crosses 3 teams', 'Result: hand-offs and delay', 'Fix: stream-aligned team owns a slice end to end'.

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas: the inverse Conway manoeuvre and its consequence, spread over separate lines without a visual of the flow.
findings.evidence: Inverse Conway manoeuvre: shape teams around the target architecture first / The architecture then follows the teams
findings.fix: Show as a one-line flow: Target architecture -> Shape teams -> Architecture emerges.

findings.summary: The ownership bullet mixes the definition with the whole-life scope, and the Design/Deploy/On-call list is unlabeled.
findings.evidence: You build it, you run it: the owning team covers the whole life of its service
findings.fix: Keep the bullet to the definition and label the Design, Deploy, On-call, Incidents, Cost list as 'Lifecycle owned by one team'.

findings.summary: The Cognitive load bullet holds two ideas (the principle and the numeric limit), and the 1-3 services limit is presented as a fixed rule without context.
findings.evidence: Cognitive load: own only what the team can fully understand and operate / Typical limit: 1-3 services per team
findings.fix: Keep the limit as its own bullet and add that it depends on service size and complexity.

findings.summary: The comparison table has very long cells that hold several ideas each.
findings.evidence: Atomic cross-service commits, one dependency version set, easy refactors
findings.fix: Split the Gives row into separate one-idea rows such as Atomic commits, Dependency versions and Refactors.

findings.summary: The CODEOWNERS code block appears before the rule it illustrates is tied to its reading, and the lines mix the path with the team.
findings.evidence: CODEOWNERS gives per-path review: each folder has its owning team
findings.fix: Keep the idea line first (already so) and state the one-line rule that the last matching pattern wins or that a path maps to a team.

findings.summary: The pipeline flow diagram is a string of labels whose direction and arrows are not stated, so it may be read as a list.
findings.evidence: Commit / SHA abc123 / Build image / tag = SHA / Staging / same artefact / Prod / same artefact
findings.fix: Render it as a left-to-right flow with arrows: Commit (SHA) -> Build image (tag = SHA) -> Staging -> Prod, same artefact promoted.

findings.summary: The Mistakes section states the result 'distributed monolith' without defining the term.
findings.fix: Add a one-line definition: services that must be released together, so they have the cost of distribution without the independence.

findings.summary: The DORA section presents four metrics as current, but DORA's 2024 report added a fifth (rework rate) and renamed 'time to restore service' to 'failed deployment recovery time'.
findings.evidence: 4 DORA metrics: frequency, lead time, failure rate, restore time
findings.fix: Say these are the four classic DORA metrics and add that the 2024 report added rework rate and renamed time to restore service to failed deployment recovery time. Apply the same change on the cheat sheet (page 6).

findings.summary: The Platform Teams anti-patterns are listed unlabeled and mixed in with the positive bullets, so a skimmer can read them as recommendations.
findings.evidence: Treats developers as customers / Measure adoption, not mandates / Ticket-queue gatekeeper for every request / Mandating tools that are not usable
findings.fix: Separate into 'Do' and 'Avoid' groups with labels.

findings.summary: DORA bullets mix an elite benchmark and a risk claim in separate lines with no numbers, and 'Elite teams deploy on demand' is a claim without a threshold.
findings.evidence: Elite teams deploy on demand, many times a day
findings.fix: Fold into the table as an 'Elite' column or drop the benchmark.

findings.summary: The cheat-sheet mistake box says splitting teams by layer gives a distributed monolith, but the chapter teaches that outcome only for lockstep releases and shared pipelines.
findings.evidence: Splitting teams by layer or shipping a lockstep release train gives a distributed monolith.
findings.fix: Separate the two consequences: 'Splitting teams by layer creates hand-offs on every feature; a lockstep release train or shared pipeline gives a distributed monolith.'

findings.summary: The Teams Shape Systems section repeats page 1 terms with different phrasing ('Self-service internals' vs 'Provides self-service internals'), and the Conway bullet is reworded from 'mirrors the communication structure' to 'becomes architecture'.
findings.evidence: Conway's law: org structure becomes architecture
findings.fix: Reuse the page 1 wording so the term has one definition.

findings.summary: Question pages state the answer immediately under each question without a way to hide it, and the second question's fix is mixed into the answer.
findings.evidence: Orders breaks at runtime: hidden coupling, and the change needed cross-team coordination. / Fix: each service owns its data and exposes an API.
findings.fix: Label each line explicitly as Q, Answer and Fix so the learner can self-test.
